title: USCGC Polar Star (WAGB 10) Ice Pilot: Operation Deep Freeze 2026
description: U.S. Coast Guard Lt. Cmdr. Daniel Jones, operations officer aboard USCGC Polar Star (WAGB 10), explains the intricacies of being an ice pilot during Operation Deep Freeze 2026, Jan. 30, 2026. Operation Deep Freeze is one of the more challenging U.S. military peacetime missions due to the harsh environment in which it is conducted, and this year also commemorates the Polar Star’s 50th year of service. (U.S. Coast Guard video by Petty Officer 2nd Class Christopher Bokum)
keywords: Coast Guard Cutter Polar Star, OperationDeepFreeze, USCG PolarOps, CGatSea, USCG, ODF26

transcript.text: Navigating through ice is an exercise
in strategic planning and patience . It
becomes really a bit of an art of
feeling your way in a tactile way
through the ice , um , reading its
movements , reading how it's going to
react to you , and anticipating the
forces that it imparts upon the ship .
Polar Star plays a crucial role in the
Antarctic region . As the US's only
heavy icebreaker , it is uniquely
capable of establishing a navigable
channel in the fast ice for fuel and
cargo ships to reach McMurdo Station ,
the largest US base on the continent
and a crucial logistics hub for the US
Antarctic program . Transiting through
pack ice is almost never accomplished
in a straight line . An ice pilot is
given extreme leeway in avoiding ice if
needed , taking leads . And choosing
lighter flows to go through as well as
avoiding glacial ice . Additionally ,
when you are navigating through regular
water , a counting officer is balancing
the ship's propulsion forces and
steering forces with fairly constant
environmental forces of wind and waves
and current , whereas an ice pilot is
dealing with extremely dynamic forces
from impacting the ice , uh , having
that ice give and create leads and
cracks . Through pressure ridges
and different types of ice every year
we utilize a wide range of optical
satellite imagery , synthetic aperture
radar , and on-scene reports to get an
idea of the conditions and extent of
the fast ice prior to our arrival .
Even with that , it is very difficult
to get an accurate picture of the exact
thickness and condition of the fast ice
prior to our arrival on scene . Once
we're here , we have to balance the
demands of the cargo and fuel vessels
that are coming in based upon their
capability in the ice , their installed
power , and their size to determine the .
Width , the angle of attack , and
the location of the fast ice channel
that we built out and that will vary
every year based upon how far out the
ice is going , if we need to make turns
in the channel , or if we need to delay
the establishment of the channel to
prevent erosion issues here on Ross
Island . For example , this year we had
a very large tanker vessel coming in ,
actually the largest , uh , so we had
to establish a much wider channel than
normal as well with uh heavy winds , we
saw a weakening of the eastern ice
plate where it attached to the land on
Ross Island . And after we established
the channel , we made the decision to
leave the brash or broken ice within
the channel to try and prevent that
eastern ice plate from coming down and
collapsing into the channel . Normally
you'd want to get rid of that ice and
kind of flush it out to allow for an
easier transit for the cargo ships ,
but by leaving it in , we prevented
that collapse even though it
necessitated a much closer of the
tanker to get her all the way into
McMurdo Station .
